MARKET.head: Wine directors plan holiday lists around familiar, approachable bottles and selective trade-ups
MARKET.summ: Even as consumer spending tightens, the holiday season is a critical time for restaurants and bars to generate wine revenue. Here’s how six sommeliers and beverage directors are prepping their cellars
takeaways: Six wine directors from across the US told SevenFifty Daily how to prepare inventory and guest expectations for the holiday season.
Directors report guests trading up one price tier, with Champagne costs rising so accessible houses like Roederer and Billecart-Salmon are favoured.
Directors say holiday guests want familiar wines and approachable options, while large-format bottles tend to boost sales for bigger parties.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads Liv-ex trade as Burgundy share falls to 15.4%
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux led Liv-ex fine wine trading with a 37.4% share of purchases, with Lynch-Bages 2005 the top-traded wine.
Burgundy's share fell to 15.4% from 18.4% the previous week, below a September average of 24.6%.
US buyers, largely for California wines, rose to 9.6% share and claimed over half of Bordeaux's purchased value.

MARKET.head: Surrey funds 17 rural projects, including a vineyard bird-repelling laser
MARKET.summ: A wine producer using bird-repelling lasers and cattle farmer using GPS collars to track livestock are among 17 innovative projects funded from a £500,000 pot to boost Surrey’s rural economy. Surrey County Council’s Farming Innovation Accelerator supports farmers and growers with funding for projects to modernise operations,...
takeaways: Surrey County Council's Farming Innovation Accelerator is giving 17 rural and farming projects grants of up to £35,000 each.
The grants come from a £500,000 pot funded by UK government Shared Prosperity Funding, drawn from over 50 proposals.
Albury Vineyard will install an automated bird-repellent laser to protect 18 acres of grapevines, adding over 1,700 bottles a year.

MARKET.head: Navarra turns demanding rosé methods into a premium selling point
MARKET.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra rosado producers use the Saignée method, needing up to three times more grapes than standard red production.
The region's Rosado Tradition designation requires Saignée and exclusively Garnacha, reinforcing premium positioning.

MARKET.head: VinePair's weekly roundup gathers drinks-industry headlines and product releases
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Heineken’s memo about effects of weight-loss drugs on drinking, RNDC’s Chapter 11 liquidation, and a ton of...
takeaways: Judge approved RNDC's Chapter 11 liquidation, per one weekly roundup.
Class action reportedly being prepared against Celsius, per the same roundup.
Roundups also cite Diageo's toxic chemical spill and a Supreme Court home distilling review.

CULTURE.head: Volcanic soils give wines a distinctive tension, importers and critics say
CULTURE.summ:
Vines on volcanic soil are hard to grow and their grapes are hard-won, but it all combines to produce wines with a very particular sense of place

Good stories need jeopardy. Take The Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced...
takeaways: Volcanic wines span ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice and tuff soils, with little stylistic common ground between regions.
Importer Nic Rizzi of Modal Wines says volcanic wines carry an extra tension, which he links to hard-working growers on La Palma.
Victoria Torres Pecis's Las Machuqueras 2016/19, from black ash soils and very old vines, retails at £55 via Modal Wines.

CULTURE.head: Plumpton College offers Level 3 viticulture apprenticeship for UK vineyards
CULTURE.summ: Develop the skills your business needs, invest in emerging talent and help shape the future of the UK wine industry with a Viticulture Apprenticeship at Plumpton College. As the UK wine industry continues to grow, developing a skilled workforce is essential to its long-term success. Plumpton College’s Level 3 Viticulture...
takeaways: Plumpton College is recruiting its next Level 3 Viticulture Apprenticeship cohort, starting 9 November, with late joiners possibly accepted in January.
For eligible non-levy-paying SMEs, the Government funds 100% of training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24, subject to funding rules.
The apprenticeship pairs workplace experience with college block weeks, and qualifications are endorsed by WineGB.

SCIENCE.head: Oak alternatives chosen by winemaking objective, with colour gains needing oxygen
SCIENCE.summ: Oak remains one of the most powerful tools available to winemakers for shaping wine style, structure, and complexity. While traditional barrel ageing continues to play an important role, modern oak alternatives offer greater flexibility, lower cost, and increased precision when used with a clearly defined objective.
takeaways: Enartis describes oak alternatives as precision tools, with toast level and surface area driving aroma release speed.
Oak chips extract rapidly, while oak tannins dissolve immediately and help bind sulphur compounds linked to off-aromas.
Colour stabilisation from oak works best during maturation with micro-oxygenation, since adding chips during fermentation gives little benefit.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards hit by 2026 frosts, then record heat that stalled Bacchus ripening
SCIENCE.summ: With harvest complete, or nearing completion on many vineyards, Hutchinsons agronomists Rob Saunders and Will Robinson look at the impact of the record-breaking summer and what we can learn for future seasons. While 2026 could be remembered as a vintage season for some growers, others will look back less fondly, having first...
takeaways: Fifty-four Met Office stations broke all-time daily maximum records this summer, including 38.2°C in Gloucestershire in August.
Older vines with deep roots coped better than young vines carrying heavy crops, and early fruit thinning helped.
Harvest came 10-14 days early, but Bacchus struggled as sugar development stalled while acidity kept falling.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards face early, hot 2026 harvest after frost and drought
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: The 2026 season began with severe frost events, then turned warm and dry, with rapid ripening across English and Welsh vineyards.
Harvest came several weeks early at some sites, and dry weather kept disease pressure low, so fruit reached wineries in good condition.
Growers now say no typical season can be planned for, so resilience must be built through soil health, water management and monitoring.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details organic and water-saving practices at Mendoza winery
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR Membership Manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet in Mendoza, at the foot of the Andes, in February.
The winery is trialing biodiversity corridors, closed to protect vegetation, and garden corridors growing vegetables between vine rows.
It switched to high-pressure hoses to clean harvest boxes and is committed to bottles under 420g via the Bottle Weight Accord.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data validated for mapping vineyard water use in Italy
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: Researchers at the University of Padova used MODIS satellite data to estimate evapotranspiration across a 25-hectare Italian vineyard.
Estimates were calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements and validated against two independent years of data.
Results showed good consistency with in situ observations, suggesting MODIS can monitor vineyard water use at regional scale.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial finds ethephon and manual thinning cut Vinhos Verdes yields
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 trial in two Vinhos Verdes vineyards tested ways to reduce yield in Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Ethephon and manual bunch thinning significantly reduced crop, with Borraçal yields falling about 41% against control under thinning.
Ethephon at berry buckshot size raised sugar and lowered acidity in Loureiro, while Borraçal showed no quality gains.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation trials show water-use gains in Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: A three-year-old Grenache vineyard in NE Spain was grafted onto three rootstocks, 110-R, 41-B and 161-49C, and tested irrigated versus non-irrigated.
Non-irrigated vines had higher water use efficiency, and 110-R and 41-B outperformed 161-49C on this measure.
Stomatal conductance differences from irrigation persisted through the season, with a positive leaf water potential link only in non-irrigated vines.

SCIENCE.head: Italian researchers outline viticulture strategies for climate change and biodiversity
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Pisa University researchers argue climate change may extend viticulture to higher latitudes and altitudes, requiring more resilient genotypes.
They say local Italian grape varieties are at risk of erosion, and some regions have started projects to recover them.
The paper reports viticultural and economic research on Latium's Malvasia, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon grown under Cordon Spur of Conegliano training.

SCIENCE.head: Conegliano pruning trials on Lazio grape varieties assess yield, quality and value
SCIENCE.summ: In this work the salient results of the viticultural and ecomomic researches earned out on interesting italic varieties of Latium (Malvasia of the Lazio and Cesanese d'Affile) and an international vsriety (Cabernet sauvignon), "Cordon Spur of Conegliano" (CSC) as growing system, will be exposed
takeaways: Researchers at Italy's CRA Viticulture Centre in Conegliano tested pruning systems on Malvasia di Lazio, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon.
Trials compared Vertical Tridimensional Minimal Pruning of Conegliano with and without DMRC, aiming to raise gross saleable product.
The study addresses vine fertility and over-cropping, which can lower wine quality, and water scarcity in Mediterranean vineyards.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Celebrating 25 years of Filipa Pato’s wines with an amazing lunch and tasting
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Flipa Pato, daughter of famous Bairrada winegrower Luis Pato, first started making her own wines 25 years ago, in 2001
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Filipa Pato, daughter of Luis Pato, began making her own wines in 2001 at age 25, now labelled with husband William Wouters.
Filipa Pato and William Wouters farm 20 hectares across 37 plots, using pigs to help regenerate soils biodynamically.
Filipa Pato uses a DJI drone to spray plant-derived preparations, despite EU rules restricting drone spraying of agrochemicals.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A New White Zin
NEWSLETTERS.summ: If you are not familiar with the lore of White Zinfandel , America’s greatest contribution to wine culture , you are missing out on some excellent cocktail conversation. I understand this might sound like the layup for a bad wine joke, but I’m not being facetious. White Zinfandel is as important to the United States
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues the US wine industry is due a sequel to White Zinfandel, which still sold 49.2 million bottles in the US in 2024.
Atkin says Sutter Home's Bob Trinchero created White Zin around 1977 when fermentation stopped early, leaving an off-dry wine that became a hit.
Atkin proposes a field-blend style called "Relevé" of mixed red and white grapes, inspired by Will Marengo's Feudal Project wine from Walla Walla.

NEWSLETTERS.head: San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex
NEWSLETTERS.summ: San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: San Francisco and its surrounding area now host a growing number of places where wine lovers can sit and drink.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A deeper look at underwater wine aging
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Is a wine from the depths ‘better’ or does it depend on the boat?
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Attis, the winery run by Robustiano Fariña's family in O Grove near Pontevedra, Galicia, ages its Albariño underwater in magnums.
The Attis Albariño 'Mar' is aged five months in the estuary at 13-16C, versus its 'Standard' bottling of about 120,000 bottles annually.
The Attis Albariño 'Mar' is sealed with a glass cap rather than cork, because cork failed under water despite waterproofing.

NEWSLETTERS.head: What to Know Before This Year’s Hospices de Beaune Wine Auction
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Discover the world's most famous charity wine auction held since 1859. Get essential tips and insights for this year's legendary Burgundy event
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: The 166th Hospices de Beaune wine sale takes place Sunday 15 November 2026, with 2026 vintage wines auctioned under the Halles de Beaune.
The 2026 Hospices crop is 432 barrels (348 red, 84 white), smaller than normal because an early heatwave reduced yields.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Owendee
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The rituals of service for the holidays, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Wine-related search queries slump in July but rise sharply through October, peaking on December 31, according to the author's search-trend evidence.
The October-to-December wine peak coincides with the Northern Hemisphere harvest, which the author says marks the start of this season.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Domaine de Beudon, a Valais estate at 890 metres, is run by the Granges-Faiss family, reached only by a hike or a cable car.
Jacky Granges-Faiss bought the estate in 1971; after his death in June 2016, Marion Granges-Faiss became the de facto winemaker.
Beudon ferments at the estate but ages and bottles at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's winery in Saillon, and whites carry 70-100 mg/L total sulphites.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Chinon's lieux-dits project, begun by the Chinon Syndicat in 2014, promotes named vineyard sites without an official hierarchy or technical criteria.
Seven lieux-dits have been officially recognized so far, starting with La Croix Boissée in Cravant-les-Côteaux in 2018.
Each recognized site requires a monograph, a collaborative study with historians, geologists and pedologists, and is marked with an engraved stone in the vineyard.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews of selections from the 2024 Port vintage after an NYC media tasting.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, with vintages from 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, held in Florence's State Archives.
A 2024 Consorzio-unveiled document shows the term Vino Nobile was first used in 1766 by the Jesuit order, not 1787 as previously thought.
In April 1806 Thomas Jefferson wrote to Thomas Appleton requesting 400 bottles annually of Montepulciano wine from the ancient Jesuit vineyards.
